claim: Autophagy facilitates the unconventional secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin 1β (IL-1β).
source: Recent evidence suggests that autophagy facilitates the unconventional secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin 1β (IL-1β).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Autophagy-regulated secretion of mature IL-1β (m-IL-1β) can be reconstituted in non-macrophage cells.
source: Here, we reconstituted an autophagy-regulated secretion of mature IL-1β (m-IL-1β) in non-macrophage cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cytoplasmic IL-1β associates with the autophagosome.
source: We found that cytoplasmic IL-1β associates with the autophagosome and m-IL-1β enters into the lumen of a vesicle intermediate but not into the cytoplasmic interior formed by engulfment of the autophagic membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from membrane fractionation and immunoisolation experiments shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: m-IL-1β enters into the lumen of a vesicle intermediate but not into the cytoplasmic interior formed by engulfment of the autophagic membrane.
source: We found that cytoplasmic IL-1β associates with the autophagosome and m-IL-1β enters into the lumen of a vesicle intermediate but not into the cytoplasmic interior formed by engulfment of the autophagic membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteinase K protection assays and STORM imaging data shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: Translocation of m-IL-1β across a membrane may require m-IL-1β to be unfolded or remain conformationally flexible.
source: In advance of secretion, m-IL-1β appears to be translocated across a membrane in an event that may require m-IL-1β to be unfolded or remain conformationally flexible and is dependent on two KFERQ-like motifs essential for the association of IL-1β with HSP90.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using DHFR fusion proteins and aminopterin treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: Translocation of m-IL-1β is dependent on two KFERQ-like motifs essential for the association of IL-1β with HSP90.
source: In advance of secretion, m-IL-1β appears to be translocated across a membrane in an event that may require m-IL-1β to be unfolded or remain conformationally flexible and is dependent on two KFERQ-like motifs essential for the association of IL-1β with HSP90.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis experiments and co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 7-8.

claim: A vesicle, possibly a precursor of the phagophore, contains translocated m-IL-1β and later turns into an autophagosome in which m-IL-1β resides within the intermembrane space of the double-membrane structure.
source: A vesicle, possibly a precursor of the phagophore, contains translocated m-IL-1β and later turns into an autophagosome in which m-IL-1β resides within the intermembrane space of the double-membrane structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by fractionation experiments in ATG2-depleted cells and STORM imaging data shown in Figures 3-6.

claim: Completion of IL-1β secretion requires Golgi reassembly and stacking proteins (GRASPs).
source: Completion of IL-1β secretion requires Golgi reassembly and stacking proteins (GRASPs) and multi-vesicular body (MVB) formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Completion of IL-1β secretion requires multi-vesicular body (MVB) formation.
source: Completion of IL-1β secretion requires Golgi reassembly and stacking proteins (GRASPs) and multi-vesicular body (MVB) formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most eukaryotic secretory proteins with an N-terminal signal peptide are delivered through the classical secretion pathway involving an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-to-Golgi apparatus itinerary.
source: Most eukaryotic secretory proteins with an N-terminal signal peptide are delivered through the classical secretion pathway involving an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-to-Golgi apparatus itinerary (Lee et al., 2004; Schatz and Dobberstein, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A substantial number of secretory proteins lack a classical signal peptide and are released by unconventional means of secretion.
source: However, a substantial number of secretory proteins lack a classical signal peptide, called leaderless cargoes, and are released by unconventional means of secretion (Nickel and Rabouille, 2009; Nickel and Seedorf, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The range of unconventional secretory cargoes encompasses angiogenic growth factors, inflammatory cytokines and extracellular matrix components.
source: The range of unconventional secretory cargoes encompasses angiogenic growth factors, inflammatory cytokines and extracellular matrix components etc. most of which play essential roles for development, immune surveillance and tissue organization (Nickel, 2003; Rabouille et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most unconventional secretory cargoes play essential roles for development, immune surveillance and tissue organization.
source: The range of unconventional secretory cargoes encompasses angiogenic growth factors, inflammatory cytokines and extracellular matrix components etc. most of which play essential roles for development, immune surveillance and tissue organization (Nickel, 2003; Rabouille et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Leaderless cargoes undergoing unconventional secretion employ multiple means of protein delivery, the details of which are largely unknown.
source: Unlike a unified route for classical protein secretion, leaderless cargoes undergoing unconventional secretion employ multiple means of protein delivery, the details of which are largely unknown (Ding et al., 2012; Nickel, 2010; Rabouille et al., 2012; Zhang and Schekman, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A biologically inactive 31 kDa precursor, pro-IL-1β, is made following initiation of the NF-κB signaling cascade.
source: A biologically inactive 31 kDa precursor, pro-IL-1β, is made following initiation of the NF-κB signaling cascade.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pro-IL-1β is converted into the active form, the 17 kDa mature IL-1β, by the pro-inflammatory protease caspase-1.
source: Pro-IL-1β is subsequently converted into the active form, the 17 kDa mature IL-1β, by the pro-inflammatory protease caspase-1 which is activated, in response to extracellular stimuli, after its recruitment to a multi-protein complex called the inflammasome (Burns et al., 2003; Cerretti et al., 1992; Rathinam et al., 2012; Thornberry et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Caspase-1 is activated, in response to extracellular stimuli, after its recruitment to a multi-protein complex called the inflammasome.
source: Pro-IL-1β is subsequently converted into the active form, the 17 kDa mature IL-1β, by the pro-inflammatory protease caspase-1 which is activated, in response to extracellular stimuli, after its recruitment to a multi-protein complex called the inflammasome (Burns et al., 2003; Cerretti et al., 1992; Rathinam et al., 2012; Thornberry et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Many reports make the case for cell lysis as a means of release of mature IL-1β.
source: Indeed, many reports including two recent publications make the case for cell lysis as a means of release of mature IL-1β (Liu et al., 2014; Shirasaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neutrophils demonstrate proper secretion of mature IL-1β without cell lysis, dependent on the inflammasome response to activate caspase-1.
source: In contrast, other reports demonstrate proper secretion of mature IL-1β without cell lysis in, for example, neutrophils, which are nonetheless dependent on the inflammasome response to activate caspase-1 and secrete mature IL-1β (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pro-IL-1β lacks a typical signal peptide.
source: Pro-IL-1β lacks a typical signal peptide and the propeptide is processed in the cytosol rather than the ER (Rubartelli et al., 1990; Singer et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The propeptide of pro-IL-1β is processed in the cytosol rather than the ER.
source: Pro-IL-1β lacks a typical signal peptide and the propeptide is processed in the cytosol rather than the ER (Rubartelli et al., 1990; Singer et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mature IL-1β secretion is not blocked by Brefeldin A, a drug that blocks the traffic of standard secretory proteins from the Golgi apparatus.
source: Although mature IL-1β appears to be incorporated into a vesicular transport system, secretion is not blocked by Brefeldin A, a drug that blocks the traffic of standard secretory proteins form the Golgi apparatus (Rubartelli et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been implicated in the unconventional secretion of IL-1β, including autophagy, secretory lysosomes, multi-vesicular body (MVB) formation and micro-vesicle shedding.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been implicated in the unconventional secretion of IL-1β, including autophagy, secretory lysosomes, multi-vesicular body (MVB) formation and micro-vesicle shedding (Andrei et al., 1999; Andrei et al., 2004; Brough et al., 2003; Lopez-Castejon and Brough, 2011; MacKenzie et al., 2001; Qu et al., 2007; Verhoef et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A clear demonstration of the mechanism for the entry of IL-1β into a vesicular carrier, e.g. the autophagosome, is lacking.
source: However, a clear demonstration of the mechanism for the entry of IL-1β into a vesicular carrier, e.g. the autophagosome, is lacking.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Macroautophagy is a fundamental mechanism for bulk turnover of intracellular components in response to stresses such as starvation, oxidative stress and pathogen invasion.
source: Macroautophagy (hereafter autophagy) is a fundamental mechanism for bulk turnover of intracellular components in response to stresses such as starvation, oxidative stress and pathogen invasion (Mizushima and Levine, 2010; Yang and Klionsky, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Autophagy is characterized by the formation of a double-membrane vesicle, called the autophagosome, through the elongation and closure of a cup-shaped membrane precursor, termed the phagophore, to engulf cytoplasmic cargoes.
source: The process is characterized by the formation of a double-membrane vesicle, called the autophagosome, through the elongation and closure of a cup-shaped membrane precursor, termed the phagophore, to engulf cytoplasmic cargoes (Hamasaki et al., 2013; Lamb et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Completion of autophagosome formation requires a sophisticated protein-vesicle network organized by autophagic factors, such as autophagy-related (ATG) proteins, and target membranes.
source: Completion of autophagosome formation requires a sophisticated protein-vesicle network organized by autophagic factors, such as autophagy-related (ATG) proteins, and target membranes (Feng et al., 2014; Mizushima et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Autophagy or ATG proteins have been implicated in multiple secretory pathways including the delivery of leaderless cargoes undergoing unconventional secretion to the extracellular space.
source: Besides the degradative function, autophagy or ATG proteins have recently been implicated in multiple secretory pathways including the delivery of leaderless cargoes undergoing unconventional secretion, such as the mammalian pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18, the nuclear factor HMGB1, and the yeast acyl coenzyme A-binding protein Acb1, to the extracellular space (Bruns et al., 2011; Dupont et al., 2011; Duran et al., 2010; Manjithaya and Subramani, 2011; Pfeffer, 2010; Subramani and Malhotra, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Golgi reassembly and stacking protein(s) GRASP(s) are required for autophagy-regulated unconventional secretion.
source: The Golgi reassembly and stacking protein(s) GRASP(s) (GRASP55 and GRASP65 in mammals, dGRASP in Drosophila, GrpA in Dictyostelium and Grh1 in yeast) are required for autophagy-regulated unconventional secretion (Giuliani et al., 2011; Kinseth et al., 2007; Levi and Glick, 2007; Manjithaya et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dupont et al., 2011 documented a role for autophagy in the secretion of mature IL-1β.
source: Dupont et al., 2011 documented a role for autophagy in the secretion of mature IL-1β (Dupont et al., 2011), but how a protein sequestered within an autophagosome could be exported as a soluble protein was unexplained.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: How a protein sequestered within an autophagosome could be exported as a soluble protein was unexplained.
source: Dupont et al., 2011 documented a role for autophagy in the secretion of mature IL-1β (Dupont et al., 2011), but how a protein sequestered within an autophagosome could be exported as a soluble protein was unexplained.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: 3D STORM demonstrated that, after entering into the autophagosome, IL-1β colocalizes with LC3 on the autophagosomal membrane.
source: Three-dimensional (3D) Stochastic Optical Reconstruction Microscopy (STORM) demonstrated that, after entering into the autophagosome, IL-1β colocalizes with LC3 on the autophagosomal membrane, which, together with an antibody accessibility assay and observations from biochemical assays, implies a topological distribution in the intermembrane space of the autophagosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: IL-1β has a topological distribution in the intermembrane space of the autophagosome.
source: Three-dimensional (3D) Stochastic Optical Reconstruction Microscopy (STORM) demonstrated that, after entering into the autophagosome, IL-1β colocalizes with LC3 on the autophagosomal membrane, which, together with an antibody accessibility assay and observations from biochemical assays, implies a topological distribution in the intermembrane space of the autophagosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by STORM imaging, antibody accessibility assays, and biochemical data shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: The distribution of IL-1β in the intermembrane space explains the mechanism accounting for its secretion as a soluble protein through either a direct fusion of autophagosome with the plasma membrane or via the MVB pathway.
source: This distribution of IL-1β explains the mechanism accounting for its secretion as a soluble protein through either a direct fusion of autophagosome with the plasma membrane or via the MVB pathway.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and known mechanisms of vesicle fusion.

claim: Generation and secretion (~5%) of mature IL-1β was achieved by co-expression of p-IL-1β and p-caspase-1 in HEK293T cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, the generation and secretion (~5%) of mature IL-1β (m-IL-1β) was achieved by co-expression of p-IL-1β and p-caspase-1 in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mature IL-1β was not produced or secreted without p-caspase-1.
source: Mature IL-1β was not produced or secreted without p-caspase-1, whereas a low level of secreted p-IL-1β (~0.2%) was detected with or without the expression of p-caspase-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A low level of secreted p-IL-1β (~0.2%) was detected with or without the expression of p-caspase-1.
source: Mature IL-1β was not produced or secreted without p-caspase-1, whereas a low level of secreted p-IL-1β (~0.2%) was detected with or without the expression of p-caspase-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Little cell lysis occurred during the treatment used to induce IL-1β secretion.
source: Furthermore, little cell lysis occurred during the treatment we used to induce IL-1β secretion: Much less precursor than mature IL-1β and little cytoplasmic tubulin was detected released into the cell supernatant during the 2 hr incubation in starvation medium (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Starvation enhanced IL-1β secretion (~3 fold).
source: Starvation, a condition that stimulates autophagy, enhanced IL-1β secretion (~3 fold) and reduced the level of IL-1β in the cell lysates (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: Starvation reduced the level of IL-1β in the cell lysates.
source: Starvation, a condition that stimulates autophagy, enhanced IL-1β secretion (~3 fold) and reduced the level of IL-1β in the cell lysates (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: Inhibition of autophagy by the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitors 3-methyladenine (3-MA) or wortmannin (Wtm) blocked IL-1β secretion activated by starvation.
source: Inhibition of autophagy by the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitors 3-methyladenine (3-MA) or wortmannin (Wtm) blocked IL-1β secretion activated by starvation and caused the accumulation of mature IL-1β in the cell (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PI3K inhibitors caused the accumulation of mature IL-1β in the cell.
source: Inhibition of autophagy by the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitors 3-methyladenine (3-MA) or wortmannin (Wtm) blocked IL-1β secretion activated by starvation and caused the accumulation of mature IL-1β in the cell (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Atg5 knockout (KO) mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs), IL-1β secretion was reduced and failed to respond to starvation.
source: Likewise, in an autophagy-deficient cell line, Atg5 knockout (KO) mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) (Mizushima et al., 2001), IL-1β secretion was reduced and failed to respond to starvation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IL-1β secretion was inhibited in a dose-dependent manner in the presence of an ATG4B mutant (C74A).
source: Moreover, IL-1β secretion was also inhibited in a dose-dependent manner in the presence of an ATG4B mutant (C74A) (Fujita et al., 2008), or after the depletion of ATG2A and B (Velikkakath et al., 2012), or FIP200 (Hara et al., 2008), which block autophagosome biogenesis at different stages (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: IL-1β secretion was inhibited after the depletion of ATG2A and B.
source: Moreover, IL-1β secretion was also inhibited in a dose-dependent manner in the presence of an ATG4B mutant (C74A) (Fujita et al., 2008), or after the depletion of ATG2A and B (Velikkakath et al., 2012), or FIP200 (Hara et al., 2008), which block autophagosome biogenesis at different stages (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: IL-1β secretion was inhibited after the depletion of FIP200.
source: Moreover, IL-1β secretion was also inhibited in a dose-dependent manner in the presence of an ATG4B mutant (C74A) (Fujita et al., 2008), or after the depletion of ATG2A and B (Velikkakath et al., 2012), or FIP200 (Hara et al., 2008), which block autophagosome biogenesis at different stages (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The reconstituted system recapitulates the autophagy-regulated secretion of IL-1β.
source: Therefore, the reconstituted system recapitulates the autophagy-regulated secretion of IL-1β.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Inhibiting MVB formation by depletion of the ESCRT components, hepatocyte growth factor receptor substrate (Hrs) or TSG101, compromised secretion of IL-1β and CD63.
source: Inhibiting MVB formation by depletion of the ESCRT components, hepatocyte growth factor receptor substrate (Hrs) or TSG101, compromised secretion of IL-1β and CD63, an exosome marker (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of the GRASP55 or GRASP65 led to the reduction of IL-1β secretion.
source: Knockdown of the GRASP55 or GRASP65 also led to the reduction of IL-1β secretion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The secretion of IL-1β in HEK293T cells depends on GRASP proteins and at least two proteins implicated in MVB formation.
source: Therefore, in addition to functions required for autophagy, the secretion of IL-1β in HEK293T cells depends on GRASP proteins and at least two proteins implicated in MVB formation, as reported previously (Dupont et al., 2011; Qu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior work.

claim: Both IL-1β and the lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II) were mainly enriched in the 25k membrane fraction.
source: Both IL-1β and the lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II), a protein marker of autophagosome, were mainly enriched in the 25k membrane fraction (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both IL-1β and LC3-II co-distributed in the L fraction at the boundary between 0.25 M and 1.1 M layer of sucrose.
source: We then separated the 25k membrane through a sucrose step gradient ultracentrifugation where both IL-1β and LC3-II co-distributed in the L fraction at the boundary between 0.25 M and 1.1 M layer of sucrose (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Further fractionation of the L fraction using an OptiPrep gradient showed co-fractionation of IL-1β with LC3-II.
source: Further fractionation of the L fraction using an OptiPrep gradient showed co-fractionation of IL-1β with LC3-II (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: IL-1β, especially the mature form, co-sedimented with autophagosomes in immunoisolation experiments.
source: To confirm the presence of IL-1β in the autophagosome, we performed immunoisolation of LC3-positive autophagosomes from the 25k fraction and found that IL-1β, especially the mature form, co-sedimented with autophagosomes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A recent study showed a colocalization of IL-1β and LC3 in the form of puncta in macrophages.
source: Consistent with our observations, a recent study also showed a colocalization of IL-1β and LC3 in the form of puncta in macrophages (Dupont et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: At least a fraction of intracellular mature IL-1β associates with the autophagosome.
source: These data demonstrate that at least a fraction of intracellular mature IL-1β associates with the autophagosome, possibly related to its role in IL-1β secretion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Depletion of ATG2 did not affect the co-fractionation of IL-1β and LC3-II.
source: Depletion of ATG2 did not affect the co-fractionation of IL-1β and LC3-II (Figure 3), indicating that IL-1β enters into the phagophore membrane before the completion of the autophagosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: IL-1β enters into the phagophore membrane before the completion of the autophagosome.
source: Depletion of ATG2 did not affect the co-fractionation of IL-1β and LC3-II (Figure 3), indicating that IL-1β enters into the phagophore membrane before the completion of the autophagosome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In control cells, p62 and a fraction of LC3-II, as well as mature IL-1β, were largely resistant to proteinase K digestion.
source: In control cells, p62 (an autophagic cargo) and a fraction of LC3-II (which was encapsulated after autophagosome completion), as well as mature IL-1β, were largely resistant to proteinase K digestion similar to the ER luminal protein, protein disulfide isomerase (PDI).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SEC22B, a membrane anchored SNARE protein exposed to the cytoplasm, was sensitive to proteinase K digestion.
source: In contrast, SEC22B, a membrane anchored SNARE protein exposed to the cytoplasm, was sensitive to proteinase K digestion (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Triton X-100 treatment permeabilized the membrane and rendered all proteins tested sensitive to proteinase K digestion.
source: Triton X-100 treatment permeabilized the membrane and rendered all proteins tested sensitive to proteinase K digestion (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The majority of membrane localized IL-1β was sequestered within an organelle, likely the autophagosome.
source: This demonstrated that the majority of membrane localized IL-1β was sequestered within an organelle, likely the autophagosome, as demonstrated by the fractionation results of Figures 2 and 3.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4A.

claim: In ATG2-depleted cells, p62 and LC3-II remained sensitive to proteinase K digestion.
source: In ATG2-depleted cells, p62 and LC3-II remained sensitive to proteinase K digestion, consistent with the hypothesis that ATG2 is essential for maturation and closure of the autophagosome (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In ATG2-depleted cells, the majority of IL-1β resisted degradation by proteinase K treatment.
source: However, in the same samples the majority of IL-1β resisted degradation by proteinase K treatment (Figure 4A), except on addition of Triton X-100 to permeabilize membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The precursor form of IL-1β remained associated with isolated autophagosome and phagophore membranes.
source: Although the precursor form of IL-1β remained associated with isolated autophagosome and phagophore membranes (Figure 3), the protein was degraded when membranes from normal and ATG2-depleted cells were treated with protease in the presence or absence of Triton X-100 (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and additional data not shown.

claim: The mature but not the precursor IL-1β appears to be transported into the phagophore.
source: Thus, the mature but not the precursor IL-1β appears to be transported into the phagophore.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4A.

claim: IL-1β was protected from proteinase K digestion in membranes from Atg5 KO MEFs.
source: Similar to what we observed in ATG2-depleted cells, IL-1β was protected from proteinase K digestion in membranes from Atg5 KO MEFs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IL-1β was sequestered within vesicles in FIP200 knockdown cells.
source: In addition, IL-1β was sequestered within vesicles in FIP200 (another early factor in phagophore development (Hara et al., 2008)) knockdown cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The entry of IL-1β into the vesicle carrier is not dependent on the formation of the autophagosome.
source: These data indicate that the entry of IL-1β into the vesicle carrier is not dependent on the formation of the autophagosome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The results are inconsistent with a role for engulfment of IL-1β by the maturing phagophore.
source: These results are inconsistent with a role for engulfment of IL-1β by the maturing phagophore and suggest instead that IL-1β may be translocated across a membrane into a vesicle precursor of the phagophore, possibly at a very early stage in the development of the organelle.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: IL-1β may be translocated across a membrane into a vesicle precursor of the phagophore, possibly at a very early stage in the development of the organelle.
source: These results are inconsistent with a role for engulfment of IL-1β by the maturing phagophore and suggest instead that IL-1β may be translocated across a membrane into a vesicle precursor of the phagophore, possibly at a very early stage in the development of the organelle.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Secretion of a mature IL-1β-DHFR fusion protein was enhanced by starvation similar to the untagged counterpart.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, secretion of a mature IL-1β-DHFR fusion protein was enhanced by starvation similar to the untagged counterpart.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: IL-1β-DHFR secretion was reduced in a dose-dependent manner in the presence of aminopterin.
source: Importantly, IL-1β-DHFR secretion was reduced in a dose-dependent manner in the presence of aminopterin (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Aminopterin did not reduce the secretion of untagged IL-1β.
source: As a control, aminopterin did not reduce the secretion of untagged IL-1β, confirming its specific effect on DHFR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Starvation led to a ~ 2 fold increase in the membrane localization and cytosolic depletion of mature IL-1β.
source: Starvation led to a ~ 2 fold increase in the membrane localization and cytosolic depletion of mature IL-1β (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Fractionation of cells incubated with aminopterin showed a reduced level of IL-1β in the membrane fraction with a corresponding increase in the cytosol fraction.
source: Fractionation of cells incubated with aminopterin showed a reduced level of IL-1β in the membrane fraction with a corresponding increase in the cytosol fraction (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The residual DHFR-tagged IL-1β associated with membranes from aminopterin-treated cells was sensitive to proteinase K digestion.
source: The residual DHFR-tagged IL-1β associated with membranes from aminopterin-treated cells was sensitive to proteinase K digestion (Figure 5D), indicating that this pool of membrane-associated IL-1β did not translocate into the lumen of the vesicle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Entry of IL-1β into a vesicle carrier involves a process of protein unfolding and translocation.
source: The data suggest that entry of IL-1β into a vesicle carrier involves a process of protein unfolding and translocation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: IL-1β contains three KFERQ-like motifs including 127LRDEQ131, 132QKSLV136 and 198QLESV202.
source: We analyzed the primary sequence of IL-1β and found three KFERQ-like motifs on IL-1β including 127LRDEQ131, 132QKSLV136 and 198QLESV202 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The 130-131AA mutant did not affect secretion of IL-1β.
source: The 130-131AA mutant did not affect secretion of IL-1β (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Q132K133 and Q198L199 mutations were both defective in secretion of mature IL-1β which instead accumulated in the cytoplasmic fraction.
source: However, the Q132K133 and Q198L199 mutations were both defective in secretion of mature IL-1β which instead accumulated in the cytoplasmic fraction (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The cytoplasmic mature forms of the mutant proteins were less abundant in the membrane fraction compared with the WT mature IL-1β.
source: The cytoplasmic mature forms of the mutant proteins were less abundant in the membrane fraction compared with the WT mature IL-1β (Figure 7C, compare the lanes without proteinase K treatment).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The membrane associated mutant IL-1β remained proteinase K accessible (less than 10% of protection compared with ~45% of WT IL-1β).
source: In addition, the membrane associated mutant IL-1β remained proteinase K accessible (less than 10% of protection compared with ~45% of WT IL-1β), demonstrating that these two KFERQ-like motifs are required for the membrane translocation of IL-1β (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The two KFERQ-like motifs Q132K133 and Q198L199 are required for the membrane translocation of IL-1β.
source: In addition, the membrane associated mutant IL-1β remained proteinase K accessible (less than 10% of protection compared with ~45% of WT IL-1β), demonstrating that these two KFERQ-like motifs are required for the membrane translocation of IL-1β (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Equal amounts of WT and mutant p-IL-1β associated with the membrane but both remained largely proteinase K accessible.
source: Equal amounts of WT and mutant p-IL-1β associated with the membrane but both remained largely proteinase K accessible (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Knockdown of Hsp90, but not of Hsp70 or Hsc70 substantially reduced IL-1β secretion.
source: Knockdown of Hsp90, but not of Hsp70 or Hsc70 substantially reduced IL-1β secretion (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Knockdown of Hsc70 compromised CMA as indicated by the stabilization of a CMA cargo, GAPDH.
source: As a control, knockdown of Hsc70 compromised CMA as indicated by the stabilization of a CMA cargo, GAPDH (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Secretion of mature IL-1β was inhibited in a dose-dependent manner by an HSP90 inhibitor geldanamycin.
source: Moreover, secretion of mature IL-1β was inhibited in a dose-dependent manner by an HSP90 inhibitor geldanamycin (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Knockdown of Hsp90 rendered IL-1β accessible to proteinase K digestion.
source: Knockdown of Hsp90 also rendered IL-1β accessible to proteinase K digestion (Figure 8C), consistent with a role for HSP90 in the translocation of IL-1β as opposed to some later secretion event.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: HSP90 associated with m-IL-1β but not the translocation-deficient mutants Q132K133 and Q198L199.
source: Furthermore, in a co-immunoprecipitation assay, HSP90 associated with m-IL-1β but not the translocation-deficient mutants Q132K133 and Q198L199 (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: p-IL-1β also formed a complex with HSP90, but the efficiency appeared lower than for m-IL-1β.
source: Although p-IL-1β also formed a complex with HSP90, the efficiency appeared lower than for m-IL-1β.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: HSP90 binds to a region of the mature IL-1β, including the essential residues Q132K133 and Q198L199, to promote the translocation event.
source: These results suggest that HSP90 binds to a region of the mature IL-1β, including the essential residues Q132K133 and Q198L199, to promote the translocation event.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Cleavage of p-IL-1β by caspase-1 may potentiate the recruitment of HSP90 to the mature form of IL-1β.
source: Cleavage of p-IL-1β by caspase-1 may potentiate the recruitment of HSP90 to the mature form of IL-1β however chaperone binding is not required for this proteolytic event (Figures 8D and 7B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 7B and 8D.

claim: Chaperone binding is not required for the proteolytic cleavage of p-IL-1β by caspase-1.
source: Cleavage of p-IL-1β by caspase-1 may potentiate the recruitment of HSP90 to the mature form of IL-1β however chaperone binding is not required for this proteolytic event (Figures 8D and 7B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 7B and 8D.

claim: IL-1β associates with HSP90 but not HSC70.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation indicated that IL-1β associates with HSP90 but not HSC70 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of Lamp2A compromised CMA but did not affect the secretion of IL-1β.
source: In addition, knockdown of Lamp2A compromised CMA but did not affect the secretion of IL-1β, and disruption of the lysosome did not result in the release of IL-1β from the membrane carrier (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Disruption of the lysosome did not result in the release of IL-1β from the membrane carrier.
source: In addition, knockdown of Lamp2A compromised CMA but did not affect the secretion of IL-1β, and disruption of the lysosome did not result in the release of IL-1β from the membrane carrier (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The translocation of IL-1β into the vesicle carrier is mechanistically distinct from CMA.
source: These data suggest that the translocation of IL-1β into the vesicle carrier is mechanistically distinct from CMA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Starvation led to a ~2.5 fold increase of the association of HSP90 and IL-1β.
source: We performed an HSP90 co-immunoprecipitation experiment with cytosol prepared from cells grown in nutrient-rich or starvation conditions (Figure 9A). Starvation led to a ~2.5 fold increase of the association of HSP90 and IL-1β (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Starvation had no effect on the cleavage of mutant forms of IL-1β unable to bind HSP90.
source: This increase was likely not due to starvation-stimulated processing of p-IL-1β because starvation had no effect on the cleavage of mutant forms of IL-1β unable to bind HSP90 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Starvation may stimulate the recruitment of a complex of m-IL-1β/HSP90 to the membrane responsible for IL-1β translocation.
source: Starvation may stimulate the recruitment of a complex of m-IL-1β/HSP90 to the membrane responsible for IL-1β translocation (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 9A and 9B.

claim: Ring-shaped autophagosomes positive for LC3 formed after starvation.
source: Ring-shaped autophagosomes positive for LC3 (cyan) formed after starvation. Some IL-1β (magenta) also organized in ring-shaped structures that co-localized with LC3 (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Some IL-1β organized in ring-shaped structures that co-localized with LC3.
source: Ring-shaped autophagosomes positive for LC3 (cyan) formed after starvation. Some IL-1β (magenta) also organized in ring-shaped structures that co-localized with LC3 (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Around 18 ring structures of IL-1β accounting for ~5% of the total IL-1β signal were observed in each cell.
source: Around 18 ring structures of IL-1β accounting for ~5% of the total IL-1β signal were observed in each cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of STORM imaging data.

claim: A 3D virtual Z-stack analysis confirmed the spatial co-distribution of LC3 and IL-1β on a ball-shaped vesicle.
source: A 3D virtual Z-stack analysis confirmed the spatial co-distribution of LC3 and IL-1β on a ball-shaped vesicle (Video 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D STORM imaging data shown in Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The diameter of the structures double-labeled with LC3 and IL-1β are ~700 nm.
source: The diameter of the structures double-labeled with LC3 and IL-1β are ~700 nm (larger structures up to 2 μm in diameter were also found) which is comparable to the size of the autophagosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of STORM imaging data.

claim: Occasionally, IL-1β was found localized in the center of the ring structure, where cytoplasmic autophagic cargoes fill, surrounded by LC3.
source: Occasionally, we also found IL-1β localized in the center of the ring structure, where cytoplasmic autophagic cargoes fill, surrounded by LC3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The portion of IL-1β in the center of the ring structure was possibly being engulfed by the autophagosome.
source: This portion of IL-1β was possibly being engulfed by the autophagosome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the STORM imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: DFCP1 was readily labeled in cells treated with digitonin alone in both WT and Atg5 KO cells.
source: Consistent with a cytosolic surface localization, DFCP1 was readily labeled in cells treated with digitonin alone (selectively permeabilizes the plasma membrane) in both WT and Atg5 KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 5A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5A-E.

claim: In WT cells, IL-1β was accessible to the antibody only after treatment with digitonin and saponin.
source: In contrast, IL-1β was accessible to the antibody only after treatment with digitonin and saponin (gently permeabilizes the endomembrane) (Figure 6—figure supplement 5A,B and F) in WT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5A, B, and F.

claim: In Atg5 KO cells, saponin treatment was necessary to expose IL-1β to antibody.
source: However, in Atg5 KO cells where the phagophore precursor envelope remains open and exposed to the cytosol, saponin treatment was necessary to expose IL-1β to antibody and roughly half of the labeled structures coincided with the phagophore marker DFCP1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 5C,D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5C, D, and F.

claim: Roughly half of the labeled IL-1β structures coincided with the phagophore marker DFCP1 in Atg5 KO cells.
source: However, in Atg5 KO cells where the phagophore precursor envelope remains open and exposed to the cytosol, saponin treatment was necessary to expose IL-1β to antibody and roughly half of the labeled structures coincided with the phagophore marker DFCP1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 5C,D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5C, D, and F.

claim: The visual assay confirms the intermembrane localization of IL-1β in the phagophore and autophagosome.
source: This visual assay further confirms the intermembrane localization of IL-1β in the phagophore and autophagosome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: U2OS cells co-expressing p-IL-1β and p-caspase-1 secreted IL-1β in a starvation-enhanced and PI3K-dependent manner similar to HEK293T cells.
source: U2OS cells co-expressing p-IL-1β and p-caspase-1 secreted IL-1β in a starvation-enhanced and PI3K-dependent manner similar to HEK293T cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Secretion of m-IL-1β-FLAG from U2OS cells was stimulated by starvation and dependent on PI3K.
source: Secretion of m-IL-1β-FLAG from U2OS cells was stimulated by starvation and dependent on PI3K (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A dual effect of autophagy has been proposed on the secretion of IL-1β in macrophages.
source: A dual effect of autophagy has been proposed on the secretion of IL-1β in macrophages (Deretic et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Induction of autophagy directly promotes IL-1β secretion after inflammasome activation by incorporating it into the autophagosomal carrier.
source: On one hand, induction of autophagy directly promotes IL-1β secretion after inflammasome activation by incorporating it into the autophagosomal carrier (Dupont et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Autophagy indirectly dampens IL-1β secretion by degrading components of the inflammasome as well as reducing endogenous triggers for inflammasome assembly.
source: On the other hand, autophagy indirectly dampens IL-1β secretion by degrading components of the inflammasome as well as reducing endogenous triggers for inflammasome assembly, including reactive oxygen species (ROS) and damaged components, which are required for the activation of caspase-1 and the production of active IL-1β (Harris et al., 2011; Nakahira et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mature IL-1β secreted by macrophages or in the surrogate cell system is completely soluble.
source: We found mature IL-1β secreted by macrophages or in our surrogate cell system to be completely soluble, thus inconsistent with the engulfment model (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Fusion of the autophagosome directly with the plasma membrane would lead to the release of soluble IL-1β available to trigger an inflammatory response in the surrounding tissue.
source: Fusion of the autophagosome directly with the plasma membrane would lead to the release of soluble IL-1β available to trigger an inflammatory response in the surrounding tissue.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and known mechanisms of vesicle fusion.

claim: If mature IL-1β were engulfed within the cytoplasmic interior of the autophagosome, fusion of this organelle at the cell surface might release an intact vesicle corresponding to the inner membrane-enclosed cytoplasmic compartment of the autophagosome.
source: If mature IL-1β were engulfed within the cytoplasmic interior of the autophagosome, fusion of this organelle at the cell surface might release an intact vesicle corresponding to the inner membrane-enclosed cytoplasmic compartment of the autophagosome.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Mature IL-1β is clearly sensitive to proteolysis.
source: Because mature IL-1β is clearly sensitive to proteolysis (Figure 4), thus any compartment engaged in presenting autophagosomal content to the cell surface must be depleted of proteases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Any compartment engaged in presenting autophagosomal content to the cell surface must be depleted of proteases.
source: Because mature IL-1β is clearly sensitive to proteolysis (Figure 4), thus any compartment engaged in presenting autophagosomal content to the cell surface must be depleted of proteases.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The unconventional secretory cargo fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) has been shown to directly translocate across the plasma membrane as a folded protein without the apparent aid of chaperones.
source: The unconventional secretory cargo fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) has been shown to directly translocate across the plasma membrane as a folded protein without the apparent aid of chaperones (Backhaus et al., 2004; Steringer et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Salvador et al. (2000) reported that DHFR fused to a CMA cargo is blocked in translocation by addition of methotrexate, a drug that stabilizes DHFR to unfolding.
source: Indeed, using a cell-free approach to study the import of CMA cargo into isolated lysosomes, Salvador et al. (2000) reported that DHFR fused to a CMA cargo is blocked in translocation by addition of methotrexate, a drug that stabilizes DHFR to unfolding, just as we have shown that IL-1β fused to DHFR is blocked in cells treated with a cell permeable folate analog, aminopterin (Wei et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IL-1β distributed in LC3-positive autophagosomal carriers that were separated from the lysosome marker LAMP2.
source: In our fractionation study, IL-1β distributed in LC3-positive autophagosomal carriers that were separated from the lysosome marker LAMP2, the proposed receptor or channel for uptake of CMA cargo (Kaushik and Cuervo, 2012) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The involvement of a different chaperone i.e. HSP90, suggests distinct routes for IL-1β and cargoes of the CMA pathway.
source: This observation, together with the involvement of a different chaperone i.e. HSP90, suggests distinct routes for IL-1β and cargoes of the CMA pathway.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 8.

claim: It is likely that a membrane receptor locating on the membrane of the vesicle carrier recruits the protein complex of HSP90 and IL-1β.
source: Although we have ruled out the involvement of LAMP2A IL-1β translocation, it is likely that a membrane receptor locating on the membrane of the vesicle carrier, perhaps a functional equivalent of LAMP2A, recruits the protein complex of HSP90 and IL-1β, therefore designating the correct membrane targeting of IL-1β.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism.

claim: A protein conducting channel may be involved in the translocation of IL-1β into the membrane.
source: In addition, a protein conducting channel may be involved in the translocation of IL-1β into the membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism.

claim: It seems unlikely that a standard translocation channel, such as SEC61, is involved in this import process.
source: It seems unlikely that a standard translocation channel, such as SEC61, is involved in this import process, but no current evidence bears on this point.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation.

claim: The exact route by which the autophagosome delivers mature IL-1β to the cell surface as well as how it avoids fusion with degradative lysosome remains obscure.
source: The exact route by which the autophagosome delivers mature IL-1β to the cell surface as well as how it avoids fusion with degradative lysosome remains obscure, possibly involving interaction with the multi-vesicular body or some form of lysosome as a prelude to fusion at the cell surface (Figure 9C), and this process may require selective recruitment of membrane sorting and targeting factors such as Rabs and SNAREs.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: The autophagosome may interact with the multi-vesicular body or some form of lysosome as a prelude to fusion at the cell surface.
source: The exact route by which the autophagosome delivers mature IL-1β to the cell surface as well as how it avoids fusion with degradative lysosome remains obscure, possibly involving interaction with the multi-vesicular body or some form of lysosome as a prelude to fusion at the cell surface (Figure 9C), and this process may require selective recruitment of membrane sorting and targeting factors such as Rabs and SNAREs.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The process of IL-1β secretion may require selective recruitment of membrane sorting and targeting factors such as Rabs and SNAREs.
source: The exact route by which the autophagosome delivers mature IL-1β to the cell surface as well as how it avoids fusion with degradative lysosome remains obscure, possibly involving interaction with the multi-vesicular body or some form of lysosome as a prelude to fusion at the cell surface (Figure 9C), and this process may require selective recruitment of membrane sorting and targeting factors such as Rabs and SNAREs.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism.
